vision.title: Build an open benchmark for intelligent survey operations
vision.lede: There are far more tiles than observing time, so every pointing is a trade-off.
paragraphs: A survey telescope has thousands of tiles it could observe each night, while the weather, target visibility and science priorities keep changing. Each choice the observer makes affects the quality of the final sample.

We want this to be an open benchmark: an agent reads the state of the night sky and decides the next observation every 15 simulated minutes. All teams get the same survey plan, weather replay, observation requests, simulator and scoring rule, so the only difference is strategy.

evaluation.title: Scoring rules
evaluation.lede: Each card is scored by the published scorer, and the card's score settings arrive in full in the initialize message. Below are the main points; section 5 of the rules has the full rules and formulas.
evaluation.formula:
total = Σ best score per target
      − 50 × missing required targets
      − 200 × (1 − J)        evenness penalty
      ± fault reports
      + rewards of completed observation requests
target score = science weight × factor × program bonus
factor = min(brightness × exposure s × sky quality ÷ (f0 × T0), 1)

criteria.desc: A target scores only if it falls in its assigned fibre's cell and stays at or above 30° altitude for the whole exposure. A target can be observed again, but only its best exposure counts. f0 × T0 is 0.5 × 900 = 450 on most cards.
If the declared program matches the target's sky band, the score is multiplied by DARK 1.20, BRIGHT 1.12 or BACKUP 1.06; otherwise by 1.00.
Each required target that is not completed costs 50 points. Completion needs a best factor of at least 0.5, and the program bonus cannot replace that threshold.
The completed fraction is computed per 10° right-ascension band and its evenness measured with Jain's index J. The penalty is 200 × (1 − J), at most 200 points.

Instrument faults never appear in bulletins or forecasts; only exposure scores reveal them. A report while an unrepaired fault exists earns 100 points and repairs it at once. After each correct report, wrong reports are free up to the card's allowance, then cost 150 each; consecutive reports have a separate cap.

A card may publish time-limited observation requests during the survey. Complete the minimum number of targets before the deadline (judged on the factor, without the program bonus) and you get the request's reward at the deadline; a missed request costs nothing. Valid exposures count automatically, with no accept action.

Each card has a budget of 900 s of normalized CPU time. Only CPU time the agent uses during its own turns counts; waiting on a model API or the network does not. There is also a 30-minute real-time cap. The survey ends when time runs out, the agent errs or it sends finish; earlier observations still score and the terminal penalties still apply.

An evaluation's result is the mean over cards A–D, and the online board is feedback only. The final ranking uses only the final version's results on the hidden cards E–H: each card is evaluated 3 times (at the same time) and averaged, then the four cards are averaged.

vision.pageSubtitle: A GOSIM Hackathon for Intelligent Survey Operations
vision.intro: This participant briefing explains why survey operations need agent observers, what a human leading observer does, how the challenge works across three planning horizons, what you submit, how scoring works, the astronomy you need, and the event schedule.

sections.title: The observing plan shapes the science sample
paragraphs: A survey telescope maps large areas of sky systematically. It does not spend a whole night on a single object; it visits thousands of tiles across many nights, building up statistically powerful samples of galaxies, quasars, and stars.

Cosmology runs on samples like these: large, uniform, well calibrated. Wide surveys reveal the large-scale structure of the universe, constrain its expansion history, underpin dark energy measurements, and tie galaxy evolution to cosmic time. Spectroscopic surveys add a third dimension — redshift. Position on the sky plus redshift gives you a three-dimensional map of cosmic structure. DESI is one concrete, public example: spectra for large samples of galaxies and quasars, used to map the expanding universe and study dark energy.

But survey operations are hard. Weather changes what a 900-second exposure is worth through seeing, transparency, and sky brightness. Target visibility shifts with airmass and position on the sky. Observing programs prefer different conditions: DARK, BRIGHT, and BACKUP. The footprint has to be covered broadly and evenly for the science to hold up. High-priority tiles, nearly finished tiles, and under-covered regions all compete for the same block of time. One bad tactical choice spends real observing time and changes every plan that follows.

Modern AI systems open a path: an assistant that reads state, calls computational tools, reasons under physical constraints, proposes a plan, monitors quality, and explains every choice. The long-term goal is an observing agent that can genuinely take part in real survey operations. This hackathon narrows that long-term vision into one focused benchmark.
sections.highlight: You build the observer’s logic. We provide the mission definition, tile table, observing constraints, weather scenarios, simulator, and evaluation protocol.

sections.title: What a human lead observer actually does
paragraphs: A seasoned lead observer makes a full set of decisions every 900-second slot: understand the science goal and decide tonight's tactical priority; read seeing, transparency, sky brightness, and the short-term forecast; judge whether tonight suits DARK, BRIGHT, or BACKUP observing; keep the tiles that are visible now, legal, and worth the time; trade off science yield, priority, airmass, footprint balance, and wasted time; finish a tile when completing it beats over-exposure; replan around weather systems, forest-fire smoke, scheduled rocket launches, and changing efficiency; use fast validation signals to calibrate later decisions; and explain why this action was chosen in this slot.

These duties are what the observing agent is taking over. We do not expect an agent to outperform a human immediately. We expect it to be evaluated objectively against a fixed interface, fixed data, and fixed scoring — so it can become a viable component of real survey operations.

sections.title: The Survey Mission Card and the challenge loop
paragraphs: Every challenge instance starts from a Survey Mission Card: the science goal, footprint area, time budget, telescope site, available observing programs, target classes, observing constraints, and scoring rules — everything a round holds you to. On this platform the mission card takes the form of published evaluation scenarios: tile catalogue, observing constraints, weather and forecasts, ad-hoc requests, simulator, and scoring configuration. The public development scenarios (dev-reference, dev-fortnight) are on the Resources page; competition scenarios are provided by the platform when the competition starts.

Every participant faces the same evaluation scenario: the overall survey plan, per-night seeing and weather replay, ad-hoc observing requests, predictable mid-term disruptions, simulator, and scoring rule are fixed. The agent receives the current state and returns the next observing action every 900 seconds.

sections.title: Plan across the survey, the week, and the next 900 seconds
paragraphs: Long term — the organizers provide the overall survey plan in the mission card, while the agent manages that plan in flight. Final scoring includes survey completeness and completion quality.

Middle term — the agent builds a flexible month, week, and day plan from progress and forecast conditions, absorbing weather systems, forest-fire smoke, scheduled launches, and newly inserted observing requests. This layer may be enabled as mission cards evolve.
Short term — every 900-second slot, the agent makes an immediate tactical choice using the middle-term plan and real-time seeing and transparency. This is the focus of the scored benchmark.

sections.title: Build a reproducibly runnable observer project
paragraphs: Any language is allowed. Submit a complete project (public repository or private ZIP) that the platform evaluates round by round in the cloud. See Docs for the interface.
The server reveals current observations step by step and scores the actual decisions. Future weather and anomaly answers remain private.
When ready, submit a complete project on Participate, then study replays to improve your strategy.
The platform keeps the full record of every evaluation — the decisions file, the run log, and a slot-by-slot replay — for organizer review, and for you to inspect why each step went the way it did.

sections.title: How scoring and the simulated environment work
paragraphs: What a completed exposure earns depends on the atmosphere and the moon at the time; matching the night's programme and answering a request add more on top. Six things cost you: unsafe observations, invalid actions, avoidable waiting, unfinished must-do patches (REQUIRED), optional shortfall per region (FLEXIBLE), and expired requests. A good agent keeps trading immediate output against coverage, weather risk, request deadlines and the time budget.

Evaluation follows open-science principles: fixed data and fixed scoring let every submitted observation result be evaluated consistently; readable result artifacts make outcomes inspectable; separate development and final-evaluation weather compare generalization instead of tuning to a known scenario.

Visualization turns completed tile fractions into an observed-target map — a 3D spatial sample and a 2D butterfly plot of sky position plus simulated redshift, in the style DESI uses — so different strategies produce visibly different maps.

The same observer interface can support future mission cards for real survey-log replay, z > 5 quasar planning, LBG planning, and target-of-opportunity inserts; the community can propose new fixed datasets for follow-up tracks.
sections.formula:
total = base_science + program_bonus + request_reward
      - unsafe_observation - invalid_action - avoidable_wait
      - required_miss - flexible_shortfall - request_miss

sections.title: A little astronomy is enough
paragraphs: You do not need an astronomy background to read the state dictionary and reason about it. A Tile is a patch of sky observed in one pointing; the Footprint is the full survey area; Targets are the object counts inside each tile. High-priority tiles carry extra scientific weight, nearly complete tiles are one exposure from completion, and under-covered regions are lagging behind the rest of the footprint.

Seeing describes atmospheric blur — lower is better. Transparency describes how clear the atmosphere is — higher is better. Sky brightness is background glow; darker is better for faint targets. Airmass measures how much atmosphere the light crosses and changes with sky position — lower is better. DARK, BRIGHT, and BACKUP are programs matched to dark, bright, and poor conditions. donefrac is tile completion: 0 means just started, 1 means finished.

The decision snapshot contains current_site_weather (observability, seeing, transparency, sky quality, instrument efficiency, active events), candidate_tiles (the legal options right now, each with geometry, airmass, lunar factor, effective weather, science value and window), active_requests, the forecasts issued so far, and progress (completed tiles, FLEXIBLE completions per region).

sections.title: Three stages from training to awards
paragraphs: The event has three stages: online training from October 2–3, online competition from October 5–7, and Awards Day at GOSIM Shenzhen on October 17. Final results are expected to be published before October 10, ahead of Awards Day.

Training covers the simulator and participant protocol; details will be announced. The competition accepts complete projects. The server reveals current information step by step and scores each complete multi-scenario batch.

Target yield, tile completion, weather response, footprint balance, and waste.
Short-term planning is primary; middle-term planning may be enabled as mission cards evolve.
Separate scenarios compare generalization instead of tuning to known weather.

scoring.principlesClosing: Future mission cards can add real survey-log replay, z > 5 quasar planning, LBG planning, and target-of-opportunity inserts. The community can propose new fixed datasets for follow-up tracks.
viz: The test data includes a deterministic table of simulated target coordinates. Each tile’s target count is bound to fixed simulated coordinates through the random seed, the tile_id, and the target class.
After a run, the simulator converts completed tile fractions into an observed-target map — how many simulated galaxies and quasars the agent actually reached.
A 3D view keeps the observed simulated universe as a spatial sample; a 2D butterfly plot folds sky position and simulated redshift together, in the style DESI uses.
Different observing strategies produce visibly different maps of cosmic structure. The visualization helps a team explain its strategy, its footprint balance, and what it missed.
scoring.vizNote: This picture is the layer built for people to look at; what is actually scored is always the planning itself.

team_env.intro_open: No model credits are provided. If your program calls a model or another external service, save the variables it needs here (API keys, endpoints, model names). During evaluation these variables are provided to your program as environment variables. You may use several providers, protocols and models at the same time; their cost is your team's.
team_env.network_open: During evaluation your program can reach any public address over HTTPS (port 443) and HTTP (port 80); no domain needs to be listed. Other ports, private and internal addresses, the local host and cloud metadata addresses are unreachable. The platform sets HTTPS_PROXY, so common SDKs need no extra configuration; programs that ignore proxy settings can connect by host name directly as well.
team_env.network_log: The platform records every address your program connects to during an evaluation (host and port, number of connections, bytes sent and received, first and last time), never any content. The record is attached to your team's run log and result files, and the organizers can see it as well. Every decision must be made by your program; no human may take part.

model_api.intro: No model credits are provided. The platform does not require a model call, but awards require agent (LLM-driven) techniques in at least two stages. If your project never calls a model, skip this section entirely. Otherwise choose how the platform handles your key:
model_api.choice: How your model key is handled
model_api.tradeoff: Saved (default): stored encrypted and deleted automatically after the results are verified. Not saved: keep this page open during evaluations.
model_api.stored_help: The key is stored encrypted on the server, so you can close this page during evaluation. It is deleted automatically after the hidden final results are published and verified.
model_api.relay_help: The key stays only in this page and is never stored on the server. Keep this page open until each evaluation finishes; model calls fail while it is closed. If your team is verified as a top team, you must also open this page at the time agreed with the organizers.
model_api.relay_deletes: Choosing this deletes the saved key.
model_api.usage: Your project keeps using the OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY provided for each run; model calls go to your endpoint. The model named in each request is forwarded unchanged; the default model is used when none is given.
model_api.limits: Each run allows up to {calls} model calls, at most {concurrency} at a time. Tokens are not capped (your team's key pays for them).
model_api.limits_tokens: Each run allows up to {calls} model calls and {tokens} tokens, at most {concurrency} calls at a time.
model_api.endpoint_hint: Any public https:// address works (an OpenAI-compatible API on the default port). IP addresses and internal addresses are not accepted. The suggestions are common providers. model_api.endpoint_refused: This API address can't be used. Use a public https:// address on the default port whose name resolves, not an IP address or an internal address.
model_api.protocol_hint: OpenAI-compatible is the default. Choose Anthropic Messages only if your provider speaks that API, and give its endpoint exactly as the Anthropic SDK expects (usually without a trailing /v1 — the SDK appends /v1/messages itself). The platform never translates between the two; a mismatched call is refused.
model_api.model_hint: Your agent may set the model parameter of each request to any model your provider offers (for example a fast, inexpensive model for simple steps and a stronger one for key decisions); the platform forwards it unchanged. Requests without a model (or with model team-model) use the default model here. Model calls are paid for by your team's key. If the provider rejects a request because it does not recognise the model name, the platform retries it once with the default model.

items.q: I am not a strong programmer. What is the minimum?
items.a: Your agent is a long-running program: at every decision it reads one JSON message (decision_request) from standard input and writes one action to standard output: observe (pointing, fibre assignments, exposure time and program), wait, report or finish. The easiest start is to download an example project from the Resources page, run it on the local practice cards, and then change its strategy. See the Docs for the protocol and how to submit.

items.q: Do I need an astronomy background?
items.a: Not much, though it helps. At the start your agent receives the site, the target catalogue (position, class, brightness, weight, required or not), the sky footprint, the fibre configuration and the scoring parameters; at every decision it receives the current time, the latest weather bulletin and forecast, new messages (such as time-limited observation requests), the result of the last exposure and the time remaining. Terms such as altitude, moonlight and the DARK/BRIGHT/BACKUP programs are explained in the Docs. You are also welcome to team up with someone who has an astronomy background.

items.q: Can I compete alone?
items.a: Yes. Create a team with a size of 1. Teams may have up to 3 members.

items.q: Which languages can I use?
items.a: Any implementation language. Both Practice and the competition take a complete project (a public GitHub repository or a ZIP), which the platform builds and runs in the cloud. The Resources page offers example projects in Python, TypeScript and Rust.

items.q: Can I use an LLM or a commercial API?
items.a: Yes, and awards require agent (LLM-driven) techniques in at least two stages. Bring your own API and quota. In the "Keys and network" section of Participate, save your keys and other variables; during evaluation they are provided to your program as environment variables, and the program can reach any public address over HTTPS and HTTP (never private or metadata addresses); the platform records the addresses it connects to (never content). Keys are stored encrypted, used only for evaluation and verification, and deleted after the hidden final results are verified; the hidden final uses them as well, with no page open.

items.q: What is the time limit per card?
items.a: Each card has a budget of 900 s of normalized CPU time (global_wallclock_seconds in the initialize message), on Practice, in the competition and on the hidden cards. Only the CPU time your agent's container uses during its turns counts (from each decision_request until your response), divided by the machine's speed factor (measured by the platform with a fixed calibration program; 1.0 = the median evaluation machine, larger = slower). Waiting on a model API or the network and platform processing are not counted. Each request's wallclock.remaining_seconds gives the budget left; plan by it. A real-time cap of 30 minutes per card stops programs that hang. There is no per-decision limit. When the budget or the cap is used up the agent is stopped, earlier observations still score and the terminal penalties apply. This timing applies to every evaluation started from 4 October 2026; earlier results remain valid.

items.q: Which task-card data are not public?
items.a: Each task card publishes its targets, sky footprint, site, telescope and fibre configuration, observing calendar and scoring parameters: practice cards α–δ can be downloaded from the Resources page now, cards A–D are published when the competition starts, and hidden cards E–H are not published before the competition ends. The actual weather of each time slot, the full forecast series, the event timeline and instrument faults are not public for any card, practice cards α–δ included; during a run your agent only receives a bulletin every 15 minutes, a forecast about once a week and other messages, and never sees future weather. The local practice cards bundled with the example projects include their full weather and event files, for local debugging and scoring only.

items.q: How many submissions can I make?
items.a: Practice: 40 complete-project evaluations per team per day (separate board). Competition: 40 evaluations per team per day, each running once on every card A–D (900 s per card), and the online board keeps your best complete evaluation. Daily quotas reset at 00:00 UTC (08:00 Beijing time); failures caused by the platform are not counted. The Practice board ranks each card separately.

items.q: Is the leaderboard score the final result?
items.a: No. The online board (October 5–7) is live feedback only. After the online phase, each team's final version is evaluated 3 times on each of the hidden cards E–H and each card is averaged; only the mean over E–H decides the final ranking. The 3 evaluations of a card run at the same time, so your model service must handle concurrent calls. We recommend making your agent behave consistently (for example with repeatable random number generation in your own program). You can check this with “Evaluate 3 times and average”. Exact ties are settled by the organizers and announced with the results. The organizers verify the top teams and expect to confirm the awards before October 10. Winning teams' entries must be released as open source.

items.q: Do I have to attend in Shenzhen?
items.a: No. The competition is online. The first- and second-prize teams are invited to the GOSIM Shenzhen conference on October 16–17 and go on stage at the closing ceremony on October 17. In principle, GOSIM covers their travel and accommodation; each team gets a booth and a roll-up banner on site. Conference staff will contact the winners with details after the competition. Remote acceptance is possible.

items.q: Is the platform free?
items.a: Yes. Registration, data and scoring are free.

items.q: Must I open-source my agent?
items.a: Award-winning entries must be released as open source.

items.q: What happens if my agent crashes or times out?
items.a: If the program crashes, exits early, or answers with a message that cannot be parsed or does not follow the protocol, the card ends with agent_error; when the 900 s run out it ends with global_wallclock_expired. In both cases the valid observations made before still score and the terminal penalties still apply. Build and run logs are under Logs for that evaluation on the Participate page, visible only to your team and the organizers. Fix the problem and resubmit within the daily limit.

items.q: Are prizes taxed?
items.a: Prize amounts are gross. Payment details are confirmed with winning teams after Awards Day.

items.q: Does the platform provide API credits?
items.a: The platform does not provide model credits. Cloud runs of complete projects use your own API key, set on the Participate page. The first 100 teams to complete the practice round (at least one successful practice score) get a Kimi perk: one Kimi Coding Plan code per team, first come, first served. Once the organizers release the codes, the captain claims it on the dashboard.

items.q: Can a Python agent use third-party libraries such as numpy?
items.a: Yes. List them in requirements.txt at the project root and put the install command in the build field of observer.project.json; the platform runs it in the build step before the evaluation starts (the build has internet access, and its time does not count toward the 900 s per card). The container's system directories are read-only, so install into the project folder, for example "build": [["pip", "install", "--no-cache-dir", "--target", ".deps", "-r", "requirements.txt"]], and set "PYTHONPATH": "/workspace/.deps" under "environment"; a plain pip install -r requirements.txt fails because the system directories are read-only. A requirements.txt without a build step is not installed automatically. While the agent runs it has no network access except the model API, so downloading or installing anything at run time will not work. The same applies to other languages, for example npm ci or cargo build. We recommend one Practice submission first to confirm that the build and run succeed.

items.q: Can my agent use several models or several providers at once?
items.a: Yes. In "Keys and network", save a key for each provider (e.g. KIMI_API_KEY, DEEPSEEK_API_KEY). Your program can then call several providers at the same time, over any protocol (OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic Messages or the provider's own API), with no domain to list, and choose the model for each request, for example a fast, inexpensive model for simple steps and a stronger one for key decisions. Model calls are paid for by your team. See the example projects' READMEs for code.

items.q: Can I do everything from the command line or let a coding agent do it?
items.a: Yes. The official survey26 command-line tool (Resources → Command-line tool) covers everything the website offers to contestants: team, keys and network, project upload, version confirmation, evaluations, logs, results, the final version and the leaderboard. Create a personal API token on your profile page and set it as SURVEY26_TOKEN. The tool has the same daily limits and quotas as the website, and every command supports --json output for programs and coding agents.

items.q: What can a personal API token do, and how do I protect it?
items.a: A token acts as your account, with exactly your permissions, daily limits and quotas; organizer functions are never available with a token, and tokens cannot create or revoke other tokens. Anyone who has the token can act as you, so do not put it in repositories, project ZIPs, logs or chats. The profile page shows when each token was last used; revoke a token there when it is no longer needed or may have been exposed, and it stops working immediately.

items.q: Which network addresses can my program reach during evaluation? Is it recorded?
items.a: Any public address over HTTPS (port 443) and HTTP (port 80); other ports, private and internal addresses, the local host and cloud metadata addresses are unreachable. The platform records every address your program connects to in each evaluation (host and port, number of connections, bytes sent and received, first and last time), never any content; the record is attached to your team's run log (agent.log) and result files (egress.json), and the organizers can see it as well. Every decision must be made by your program; external services must not be used to bring a human into the decisions.

protocol.title: Protocol at a glance

desc.initialize: Sent once on stdin before the clock starts, no reply expected: calendar, site, the full tile and target catalogue with tile_science_value, the scoring contract and global_wallclock_seconds.
desc.decision_request: Sent once per decision: the cursor, the current slot's site weather, the candidate tiles with geometry, lunar factor and effective weather, the active requests, night and weekly publications when due, and your progress. Never any future weather.
desc.decision_response: Your agent replies with one JSON line carrying the same decision_sequence: observe a tile in a program (optionally tagged with a request_id), or wait out the slot.

protocol.truncated: Real messages from the 14-night reference run; long arrays are truncated with "… more" markers.
